items.readable_text:
Content:
We can apply our graphing calculator's root-finding capabilities to accurately approximate a point of intersection of two curves.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following functions:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=x^4-1, \qquad g(x)=\sqrt x]

Content:
A sketch of the functions and their common intersection point is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1afcca314dca4f437a233b556c68cd88]

Content:
While it may be tempting to approximate the intersection point by plotting the two functions on a graphing calculator, it's often easier and more accurate to reduce the problem to one that involves finding roots.

Content:
To find the [MATH: x]-values of the intersection point, we need to solve the equation

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = g(x).]

Content:
This equation can be written as

Content:
[MATH: f(x)-g(x)
= 0.]
Therefore, the problem can be reduced to finding the roots of the function [MATH: h(x),] given by

Content:
[MATH: h(x)|= f(x) − g(x); = (x^{4} − 1) − (sqrt(x)); = x^{4} − 1 − sqrt(x).]

Content:
The function [MATH: h(x)] and its root are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0d7f4079a834fdc154bb21bf1d3150a0]

Content:
We can now apply the usual root-finding techniques to find a good approximation of the root of [MATH: h(x).] The [MATH: x]-coordinate of the root corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point of [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x).]

sections.normalized_html: Find the number of solutions of the equation [MATH: e^{-x^2} = \sin 3x] on the interval [MATH: x \in \left[0,3\right].]
sections.readable_text: Find the number of solutions of the equation [MATH: e^{-x^2} = \sin 3x] on the interval [MATH: x \in \left[0,3\right].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The solutions of the equation correspond to the [MATH: x]-coordinates of the intersection points between the curves

[MATH: f(x)=e^{-x^2}, \qquad g(x)=\sin 3x.]

The [MATH: x]-values of the intersection points are given by the equation

[MATH: f(x) = g(x)]

which can be written as

[MATH: f(x)-g(x) = 0.]

As a result, the problem can be reduced to finding the roots of the function

[MATH: h(x)|= f(x) − g(x); = e^{− x^{2}} − \sin 3x.]

First, we plot [MATH: y=h(x)] using a graphing calculator. Since [MATH: h(x)] contains trigonometric functions, you need to make sure your calculator is in [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{RAD}\,}] (radians) mode.

To plot the function, we press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,y=\,}] and enter the function definition in the first available space. We then press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{graph}\,}] to graph the function.

We can adjust the window settings using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{window}\,}] button (or equivalent).

In our case, the appropriate window ranges could be the following:

  • for the horizontal axis, [MATH: x \in [0, 3]]

  • for the vertical axis, [MATH: y \in [-2,2]]

This gives us the following graph:

From the graph, we see that [MATH: y=h(x)] has [MATH: 3] roots in the interval [MATH: x\in [0,3].]

Therefore, the equation [MATH: e^{-x^2} = \sin 3x] has [MATH: 3] solutions on the interval [MATH: x \in \left[0,3\right].]

sections.normalized_html: Find an approximation for the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point between the curves [MATH: f(x) = x^3 + 2x + 3, \qquad g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}] that lies to the right of the [MATH: y]-axis.
sections.readable_text:
Find an approximation for the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point between the curves
[MATH: f(x) = x^3 + 2x + 3, \qquad g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}]
that lies to the right of the [MATH: y]-axis.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the [MATH: x]-values of the intersection points, we need to solve the equation [MATH: f(x) = g(x)] which can be written as [MATH: f(x) - g(x) = 0.]

As a result, the problem can be reduced to finding the roots of the function [MATH: h(x)|= f(x) − g(x); = x^{3} + 2x + 3 − (1)/(x).]

First, we plot [MATH: y = h(x)] using a graphing calculator to find an interval that contains the root.

To plot the function, we press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,y=\,}] and enter the function definition in the first available space. We then press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{graph}\,}] to graph the function.

To get a better view, we might need to either

  • zoom in or out, or

  • adjust the window ranges.

We can adjust the window settings using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{window}\,}] button (or equivalent).

In our case, the appropriate window ranges could be the following:

  • for the horizontal axis, [MATH: x \in [-2, 2]]

  • for the vertical axis, [MATH: y \in [-2,4]]

This gives us the following graph:

The graph shows that the root lies inside the interval [MATH: x \in [0,1].]

To get a good approximation for the root, we use the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{zero}\,}] command (or equivalent). This is usually accessed by pressing the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{calc}\,}] button (or equivalent). Note that we sometimes need to press the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{2nd}\,}] or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{shift}\,}] button first.

We enter the following when prompted:

  • The "left bound" should be a value close to the root on its left-hand side. Let's pick [MATH: 0.]

  • The "right bound" should be a value close to the root on its right-hand side. Let's pick [MATH: 1.]

  • The "guess" could be any number from [MATH: (0,1).] Let's pick [MATH: 0.3.]

The calculator returns the zero

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x \approx 0.279\,299.]

Rounding to [MATH: 3] decimal places, we obtain the following:

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: x \approx 0.279]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can apply our graphing calculator's root-finding capabilities to accurately approximate a point of intersection of two curves.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following functions:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=x^4-1, \qquad g(x)=\sqrt x]

Content:
A sketch of the functions and their common intersection point is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1afcca314dca4f437a233b556c68cd88]

Content:
While it may be tempting to approximate the intersection point by plotting the two functions on a graphing calculator, it's often easier and more accurate to reduce the problem to one that involves finding roots.

Content:
To find the [MATH: x]-values of the intersection point, we need to solve the equation

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = g(x).]

Content:
This equation can be written as

Content:
[MATH: f(x)-g(x)
= 0.]
Therefore, the problem can be reduced to finding the roots of the function [MATH: h(x),] given by

Content:
[MATH: h(x)|= f(x) − g(x); = (x^{4} − 1) − (sqrt(x)); = x^{4} − 1 − sqrt(x).]

Content:
The function [MATH: h(x)] and its root are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0d7f4079a834fdc154bb21bf1d3150a0]

Content:
We can now apply the usual root-finding techniques to find a good approximation of the root of [MATH: h(x).] The [MATH: x]-coordinate of the root corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point of [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x).]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Number of Solutions to an Equation on an Interval

Example Prompt:
Find the number of solutions of the equation [MATH: e^{-x^2} = \sin 3x] on the interval [MATH: x \in \left[0,3\right].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The solutions of the equation correspond to the [MATH: x]-coordinates of the intersection points between the curves

[MATH: f(x)=e^{-x^2}, \qquad g(x)=\sin 3x.]

The [MATH: x]-values of the intersection points are given by the equation

[MATH: f(x) = g(x)]

which can be written as

[MATH: f(x)-g(x) = 0.]

As a result, the problem can be reduced to finding the roots of the function

[MATH: h(x)|= f(x) − g(x); = e^{− x^{2}} − \sin 3x.]

First, we plot [MATH: y=h(x)] using a graphing calculator. Since [MATH: h(x)] contains trigonometric functions, you need to make sure your calculator is in [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{RAD}\,}] (radians) mode.

To plot the function, we press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,y=\,}] and enter the function definition in the first available space. We then press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{graph}\,}] to graph the function.

We can adjust the window settings using the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\text{window}\,}] button (or equivalent).

In our case, the appropriate window ranges could be the following:

- for the horizontal axis, [MATH: x \in [0, 3]]
- for the vertical axis, [MATH: y \in [-2,2]]

This gives us the following graph:

[IMG: /graphics/5698745e0df1cf8348ca19db97ee1ef4]

From the graph, we see that [MATH: y=h(x)] has [MATH: 3] roots in the interval [MATH: x\in [0,3].]

Therefore, the equation [MATH: e^{-x^2} = \sin 3x] has [MATH: 3] solutions on the interval [MATH: x \in \left[0,3\right].]
